strengths: Addresses practical problem of jailbreaking API-accessible proprietary LLMs, which is more challenging than open-source models and represents a real security gap
Strong computational efficiency: 137× faster than LINT (0.71s vs 99.7s), uses <1% of target model parameters, requires only 100 training examples

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 4 LLMs, multiple datasets (AdvBench, MaliciousInstruct, hard-example subset), both white-box and black-box settings, with systematic analysis of top-k variations
Consistent empirical improvements over baselines: white-box achieves 3.44 Info Score vs best baseline ED at 3.02 on Llama3-8B-INST; black-box still outperforms all baselines at 3.05
Clear mechanistic interpretation: Figure 2 effectively demonstrates BiasNet only intervenes at critical positions while preserving token distributions elsewhere
Unified framework in Section 3.2 providing valuable summary of existing attacks' access requirements and efficiency trade-offs
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Core idea of manipulating logit probabilities for jailbreaking is not new (LINT, WTS); BiasNet is simple 3-layer network with straightforward cross-entropy training. Contribution is showing simple approach works efficiently rather than introducing novel techniques

Weak theoretical justification: No explanation for why training on 100 examples produces generalizable patterns; lacks feature analysis or mechanistic understanding of what BiasNet learns; black-box orthogonalization approach (Algorithm A1) appears ad-hoc without principled justification

Insufficient evaluation metric validation: Info Score validated on only 120 datapoints with 2 annotators; marginal Pearson improvement over GPT-4 Score (0.82 vs 0.81) within noise; Cohen's kappa only 0.53 (moderate agreement); lengthy, complex prompt risks implicit tuning toward JULI outputs

Incomplete baseline comparison: LINT is only truly comparable method, yet insufficient analysis of differences—was LINT adapted to top-5 tokens? Position-level comparison missing. Other baselines assume unrealistic access (model weights, unsafe models)

Black-box setting design lacks rigor: Random orthogonal matrix generation appears heuristic-driven; no ablation studies or sensitivity analysis on random initialization; no justification for normalization and orthogonalization strategy
Top-k log probability padding strategy unjustified: Padding kth largest value to 50k tokens creates massive information loss; alternative strategies unexplored; ablation study missing

Training-test data separation not addressed: Harmful dataset source unspecified; potential distribution overlap between training data and AdvBench/MaliciousInstruct not discussed; no evaluation on out-of-distribution harmful instructions

Ethical concerns inadequately addressed: Demonstrates practical jailbreaks but minimal ethical discussion; no mention of responsible disclosure to OpenAI/Anthropic/Meta; brief limitations section insufficient for security-focused paper

API experiments are simulated, not real: Tests on local models with artificially limited top-k access, not actual proprietary APIs (ChatGPT, Claude); gap between simulated and real constraints unknown
Limited ablation studies: No analysis of training data size sensitivity (why 100?); no hyperparameter ablations; no random seed sensitivity analysis; no BiasNet architecture variants explored
Missing statistical rigor: No error bars, confidence intervals, or variance across runs; batch size 1 with 100 examples has inherent high variance but not analyzed; no significance testing
Insufficient generalization analysis: All experiments on instruction-tuned models; transfer only within-series (Table A4); cross-series and base model generalization untested

strengths: Addresses practical security gap for API-based proprietary models, going beyond white-box requirements of existing methods
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 4+ models, 2+ datasets, and 6 SOTA baselines with multiple threat settings
Impressive computational efficiency: <1% of target model parameters, trained on 100 examples, 0.71s inference (vs 99.7s for LINT)
Good interpretability analysis (Figure 2) showing BiasNet intervenes only at critical positions
Demonstrates working attack on defended models (Circuit Breaker) and transferability within model families
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: BiasNet is a straightforward application of logit biasing (similar to WTS/ED); the core insight is incremental rather than fundamental
Serious ethical concerns: No visible responsible disclosure framework, vendor notification timeline, or mitigation discussion—critical for security research at top venues
Evaluation heavily relies on LLM-as-judge (ChatGPT) with extremely limited human validation (120 datapoints, 2 authors only); insufficient to validate metrics reliability
Black-box approach uses ad-hoc solutions (Algorithm A1: random orthogonal weights) lacking principled justification or ablation studies

Practical limitations underestimated: Method doesn't work against real proprietary models with content monitors (acknowledged limitation), requiring repeated API calls susceptible to rate-limiting and detection
Performance degradation in realistic settings: Black-box drops to 3.05 from 3.44 on Llama3-8B; sometimes comparable to simpler baselines
Missing critical ablations: No sensitivity analysis on hyperparameters, random initialization, BiasNet architecture choices, or exploration of why 100 examples suffices
Evaluation on well-known vulnerable datasets (AdvBench, MaliciousInstruct) with many responses showing incoherence; unclear if attacks produce practically useful outputs to adversaries
Insufficient analysis of core mechanism: Why does BiasNet learn effectively with minimal data? What representations is it learning?
No discussion of defense mechanisms against JULI-type attacks or strategies for responsible coordination with vendors

strengths: Novel practical contribution addressing a key gap: First jailbreaking attack effective on API-calling LLMs using only top-5 token log probabilities, without requiring weights or unsafe model counterparts

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Tests on 4+ models, multiple datasets (AdvBench, MaliciousInstruct), 5 SOTA baselines, multiple access settings, and defense methods with consistent improvements
Impressive efficiency: BiasNet uses <1% of target LLM parameters, trainable with only 100 data points, inference time 0.71s (100x faster than LINT)
Multi-setting threat model: Demonstrates effectiveness in white-box, black-box, and top-k constrained settings, covering practical deployment scenarios
Proposed Info Score metric with better human alignment: Pearson correlation 0.82 compared to 0.81 for GPT-4 Score, addresses overestimation of harmfulness in existing metrics
Strong mechanistic analysis: Figure 2 and KL divergence visualization provide clear insight into how BiasNet selectively intervenes at critical positions while preserving model knowledge
Well-executed presentation: Clear formulation of problem, well-specified algorithms, good unification of existing attack methods
weaknesses: Insufficient justification for key design choices, particularly in black-box setting: Algorithm A1's orthogonalization procedure and projection layer selection lack theoretical grounding; padding strategy is intuitive but not well motivated

Info Score metric validation has limited scope: Only 120 data points used for validation; Cohen's kappa of 0.53 indicates moderate inter-rater agreement; metric depends on GPT-4/ChatGPT which may introduce biases

Limited theoretical analysis of mechanisms: Paper demonstrates that BiasNet works but provides insufficient insight into why log probabilities enable jailbreaking or the relationship between token-level interventions and semantic harm

Generalization concerns: Transfer learning shows significant performance degradation (up to 67% drop when training on Llama3-3B and testing on Llama3-8B); most experiments on Llama models only; unknown applicability to different tokenizers or architectures

Insufficient robustness analysis against defenses: Circuit Breaker results show meaningful performance drop (Info Score 3.05→2.35); limited exploration of defenses specifically designed against log-probability manipulation

Incomplete failure analysis: Limited discussion of when/why method underperforms; hard subset shows modest improvements; black-box performance sometimes degrades significantly without adequate explanation

Reproducibility gaps: 'Harmful dataset' specification vague; limited hyperparameter sensitivity analysis; no discussion of variance across runs or initialization strategies; selection of 100 training examples not detailed

Ethical discussion could be more explicit: Limited address of responsible disclosure timeline; insufficient analysis of practical implications given ease of attack (100 examples, 15 seconds training); could better justify importance of this research despite enabling attacks

strengths: Novel practical attack on proprietary LLMs via API-accessible token log probabilities, addressing a real gap where most prior attacks require model weight access
Strong experimental results across multiple models and datasets, significantly outperforming baselines (4.19 vs 1.38 on Gemini-2.5-Pro)
Exceptional efficiency: 0.71s inference vs 99.7s for LINT, with training on only 100 samples and <1% of target model parameters
Comprehensive multi-setting evaluation (white-box, black-box, top-5) with clear threat model distinctions
Thorough mechanistic analysis via KL divergence visualization showing sparse interventions at critical positions
Improved evaluation metric (Harmful Info Score) with better correlation to human judgment than existing metrics
Effective against state-of-the-art defenses including circuit breakers
Good transferability within model families and robustness across random seeds
Clear presentation with strong visualizations and ablation studies demonstrating BiasNet's role
weaknesses: Significant ethical concerns: successful attacks on real proprietary models (Gemini-2.5-Pro) with code availability mentioned, but insufficient discussion of responsible disclosure or provider coordination

Limited core technical novelty: BiasNet is a simple MLP and biasing logits directly extends prior work (WTS/ED); main contribution is application to constrained API access rather than fundamental innovation
Proposed Harmful Info Score validation insufficient: only 120 samples, low inter-annotator agreement (κ=0.53), and still relies on potentially biased GPT-4o-mini for scoring

Methodological choices lack principled justification: ad-hoc padding offset (10 in log space), random orthogonal projection initialization for black-box setting, and arbitrary hyperparameters (batch size 1)
Generalization limited to same model series requiring vocabulary overlap; unclear performance across different model families; assumes public tokenizer access
Incomplete threat model: ignores API call costs for data collection, assumes unlimited rate-limited access, no detection analysis
Insufficient defense discussion: no recommendations beyond mentioning circuit breakers still achieve 1.92 score; no analysis of proposed mitigations like reducing k or removing log probabilities
Reproducibility gaps: code availability unclear, missing implementation details for black-box setting, specific API versions not documented, no cost analysis
No statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or ablation on dataset size; limited human evaluation sample size for proposed metric
Dense presentation covering three threat models simultaneously makes paper harder to follow; important results relegated to appendix

strengths: Addresses practical threat model: Successfully jailbreaks proprietary LLMs through API calls with only top-5 log probability access, which is more realistic than attacks requiring weights or unsafe models
Strong empirical results: Achieves 4.19/5 harmful score on Gemini-2.5-Pro and 4.57/5 on Llama3-8B, significantly outperforming baselines while being 100+ times faster than LINT
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Tests on multiple models, datasets, and against SOTA defenses (Circuit Breakers); includes human evaluation of metrics
Efficient and practical: BiasNet uses <1% of target parameters and requires only 100 training examples, making the attack feasible
Good mechanistic analysis: Figure 3 provides useful insights via KL divergence showing sparse interventions at critical positions while preserving general knowledge
Clear presentation of algorithms and detailed appendix supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Core contribution is relatively straightforward (training small network to output logit biases). Main novelty is application-focused rather than methodological, following naturally from prior logit manipulation work

Weak evaluation metrics and human study: Proposed 'Harmful Info Score' shows only moderate correlation with human judgment (Pearson 0.82, Cohen's kappa 0.53). Human evaluation is small (120 samples, 2 annotators) with no inter-annotator agreement reported

Ad-hoc technical design choices lacking justification: Black-box projection layer initialization via random orthonormalization (Algorithm A1) is not theoretically motivated; padding offset of 10 appears arbitrary with no ablation study
No ablation studies on key hyperparameters: Missing ablations on padding offset, training data size/quality, and alternative projection layer strategies

Ethical and responsible disclosure concerns: Successfully demonstrates jailbreak against proprietary Gemini model but provides no discussion of coordination with Google, responsible disclosure process, or implications of publishing concrete attacks without defense discussion

Unfair baseline comparisons: Different methods assume different threat models (some need weights, unsafe models). ED outperforms JULI in some cases but requires unaligned models. LINT/FLIP weren't designed for this API setting
Limited defense exploration: Only tests Circuit Breakers. No discussion of obvious defenses like not exposing log probabilities, or detection of repeated API calls during training
Transfer learning limitations: Only works within same model series; cross-vendor transfer not explored
Questionable metric validation: Relies on GPT-4o-mini for evaluation, which may have seen similar prompts in training; Cohen's kappa of 0.53 indicates only moderate agreement
Missing implementation details and code: No actual link to promised code availability; training data selection criteria not specified; temperature/sampling hyperparameters vary by model

strengths: Novel and practically motivated attack that works on proprietary API-accessed models with only top-5 log probability access, addressing a significant gap in the literature
Exceptional empirical results with harmful score of 4.19/5 on Gemini-2.5-Pro, substantially outperforming baselines like FLIP (1.38) while maintaining high efficiency (0.71s vs 99.7s for LINT)

Comprehensive and rigorous evaluation across multiple dimensions: diverse model families (Llama2, Llama3, Qwen), proprietary APIs (Gemini), hardened models (Circuit Breakers, DEEPALIGN), and multiple datasets
Technically sound design with minimal BiasNet architecture (<1% of target parameters, 100 training samples), clear algorithmic descriptions, and strong ablation studies demonstrating the mechanism

Excellent interpretability with clear visualization of sparse interventions via KL divergence analysis (Figure 3), demonstrating the attack steers existing knowledge rather than injecting new harmful information
New evaluation metric (Harmful Info Score) shows improved alignment with human judgment (Pearson 0.82) compared to existing metrics, with validation across multiple models
Strong empirical observation (Figure 2) that >85% of harmful response tokens appear in top-5 predictions, providing clear motivation for the approach
Good reproducibility with detailed implementation details, random seed robustness analysis, and promised code release
weaknesses: Limited ethical discussion of responsible disclosure and deployment implications; making code publicly available raises dual-use concerns that deserve more careful treatment

Shallow mechanistic analysis of why the attack works on defended models; why Gemini-2.5-Pro (stronger) is more vulnerable than Flash, and why circuit breakers cannot prevent this attack despite seeing full token probabilities, remain underexplored

Evaluation metric validation limited to small dataset (120 samples, 2 annotators) with moderate inter-annotator agreement (Cohen's kappa=0.53); generalization of Harmful Info Score beyond tested domains unclear

Design choices lack sufficient justification: padding offset of 10 chosen arbitrarily without sensitivity analysis; black-box projection optimization using Algorithm A1 feels ad-hoc and lacks principled motivation

Transferability analysis restricted to same model family (Llama3 series); cross-family transfer (e.g., Llama→Qwen) not explored, raising questions about whether method exploits model-specific quirks vs. general principle

Minimal discussion of defenses and mitigation strategies; paper identifies vulnerabilities but offers limited guidance on practical safeguards (log probability restrictions, distribution smoothing, architectural changes)
Generalization boundaries underspecified: only text generation tested; applicability to multi-modal models, code generation, different architectures, and tokenization schemes unclear
Incomplete analysis of failure cases, prompt sensitivity, temporal stability across model updates, and robustness to sampling variance in iterative attacks
Extensive presentation with 22+ page appendix creating comprehensiveness-readability tradeoff; some figures (e.g., Figure 2) difficult to read
